stem: A client has persistent painless lymph-node enlargement, unexplained fever, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss. A lymph-node biopsy shows Reed-Sternberg cells. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
rationale: NCI describes Hodgkin lymphoma as a lymph-system cancer marked by Reed-Sternberg cells. Common manifestations include painless swollen lymph nodes, fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, and fatigue, and lymph-node biopsy is used in diagnostic evaluation. Therefore B is the best answer. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can also cause lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms, but it is not defined by Reed-Sternberg cells. Acute leukemia and multiple myeloma are different hematologic malignancies and do not fit the defining biopsy finding in this stem.
educational_objective: Recognize Hodgkin lymphoma when persistent painless lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms are accompanied by Reed-Sternberg cells on lymph-node biopsy.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Hodgkin Lymphoma Treatment (PDQ®) — Patient Version; NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms — Hodgkin lymphoma
source_version_date: Current NCI PDQ and Dictionary content rechecked 2026-08-17
source_locator: PDQ > General Information About Hodgkin Lymphoma > signs and symptoms; diagnostic evaluation/lymph-node biopsy and Reed-Sternberg cells; NCI Dictionary > Hodgkin lymphoma definition: marked by Reed-Sternberg cells
source_claim_supported: Hodgkin lymphoma commonly causes painless swollen lymph nodes, fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, and fatigue; Reed-Sternberg cells are characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma and can be identified in lymph-node tissue during diagnostic evaluation.

correction_summary: The original symptom cluster was not specific enough because NCI also lists swollen nodes, fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, and fatigue for non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Added the defining source-supported lymph-node-biopsy finding of Reed-Sternberg cells and changed the keyed diagnosis from generic 'lymphoma' to Hodgkin lymphoma. Replaced weak nonhematologic distractors with parallel hematologic malignancies. Difficulty reduced from hard to moderate.
